body: Six days a week for nineteen years, the fruit stall has gone up in the dark. Twenty past five in the morning, and the man setting it out has the radio propped on an upturned crate, because the crate is the only thing at the right height. He is not listening to it. He is counting boxes and swearing gently at a stack of trays that will not sit flat. A song finishes, and a voice says the thing it says at this hour, and the man three stalls down — who is doing his own boxes, with his own radio, and who has not looked up — says the last four words of it at exactly the same moment. Neither of them acknowledges this. It happens most mornings.

There is only one reason two men forty feet apart can do that. They are not each being served something. They are both being sent the same thing, at the same instant, by somebody who decided in advance what it was going to be.
Every live station on this band plays from a schedule written out and published before it airs. Tune in at a given second and you hear exactly what everybody else tuning in at that second hears.

It is worth being precise about what published in advance actually means, because it sounds like an operational detail and it is closer to a moral position. It means the schedule is a document that exists before the audio does. It can be read. It can be checked against the catalogue. It can be disagreed with by somebody who thinks the wrong thing has been put in the wrong hour, and that disagreement can happen while there is still time to act on it. A station assembled as it goes cannot be argued with, because until the moment it plays there is nothing there to argue with.

There are 46 frequencies on air across a dial running from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70, and every one of them has a day. Gospel Country opens with Country Gospel Morning at seven and closes with the Front-Porch Hour at six. Midnight Praise runs The Long Night from ten and the Watch of the Fourth Hour from three.

Writing that down is work, and it is work that nobody thanks you for. A shuffle is free. It fills every hour of every station for ever at no cost, and it never has to be answerable for any of them. A published schedule means somebody has to have an opinion about four o’clock on a Tuesday morning, when the audience is smallest and the temptation to let the machine handle it is greatest — and having published it, they cannot quietly improve it afterwards and pretend it was always that way. The hours nobody is watching are exactly the hours a schedule makes you responsible for.

The alternative has become so normal that it is nearly invisible. Almost every surface a person meets now is personalised: the feed, the queue, the front page, the recommendations, all of it assembled per head and different for everybody. It is presented as attentiveness and it is genuinely convenient. But the effect at scale is that no two people are any longer in the same room, and nobody can tell, because everybody’s room looks fine from the inside.

So the schedule here is allowed to do the things only a schedule can. A morning can sound like morning and a midnight can sound like midnight. The hero slot can go to a Shabbat station from Friday sundown, because the calendar knows where sundown is. A Scripture reading can be put where it will be caught rather than where it will be skipped past. None of that is available to a system that decides what is next only once you have arrived.
Be fair to shuffle first. It has real virtues, and pretending otherwise would be a cheap way to win.

A shuffle will almost never play you something you actively hate, and if it does you are three seconds from the end of it. It fills a silent room instantly. It costs nothing to run and it needs nobody awake at four in the morning. Against all that, a published schedule looks like an antique. But a shuffle cannot make a morning, because it does not know it is morning; it cannot be shared, because there is no it to share; and it cannot be inspected, because it does not exist until it happens. A shuffle gives everybody their own private radio station. That sounds generous, and it dissolves the one thing radio was for.
A shuffle can be pleasant. It cannot be simultaneous.

A woman in her fifties puts the kettle on at nine in the evening and turns the radio on in the kitchen, which is not unusual, except that she does it at nine exactly. Her son moved abroad two years ago and it is four in the afternoon where he is, and he has the same frequency on in a small flat with the window open. They did not make much of the arrangement when it started. They do not talk while it is on, and they are not on the telephone; the whole thing would collapse if either of them tried to explain it. She hears a song, and knows he is hearing it, and gets on with washing a pan. Some weeks that is the entire contact they have.

Nothing about that requires a feature. It requires only that the station be the same station for both of them at the same second, which is the one thing personalisation is constitutionally unable to provide.

The price is genuinely paid by the listener, and it should be named rather than glossed. You will arrive in the middle of things. You cannot skip, you cannot rewind, and you cannot ask for the other one. At three in the morning you will get the three in the morning hour whether or not it suits your mood, and some nights it will not. A schedule can be wrong for you in a way a shuffle never is, because a schedule was written for a station rather than for you.

That exposure is the whole substance of the format. A thing that can never be wrong for you can also never be right for you in any way that counts, because it has never taken the risk of deciding anything. Everything worth having on a broadcast band comes from somebody else being in charge of the next three minutes — the song you would not have chosen, the reading that landed at the wrong moment and turned out to be the right one, the sense that this hour was made for something and you have walked into it. Being served is comfortable. Being sent something is what changes people.

So the schedule is not the paperwork behind the band; it is the band. Written before it airs, it can be inspected. Existing before it plays, it can be shared. Nothing reaches the air that is not in the catalogue, what is going out is knowable in advance rather than only afterwards, and two strangers can hear the same thing at the same instant and be, however briefly, in the same room.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every live one of them runs to a written day.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 309.30 — Gospel Country. It is where a published day is easiest to hear, because it happens in ordinary daylight hours rather than at some romantic hour of the night: Country Gospel Morning at seven, when a great many people are doing what the man with the fruit stall was doing, and the Front-Porch Hour at six, when they have stopped. Nothing about either is assembled for you on arrival. Both were written down before they played, and the front porch at six is the same porch for everybody sitting on it — which is the entire property this article has been arguing for, running in the least exotic part of the schedule.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a case to accept. Do not curate it, and do not build yourself a queue — those are library words, and this is a band. Put HM 309.30 on tomorrow morning while you are getting the day started, and let it hand you whatever it had already decided to hand everybody. Somewhere out there a stranger is getting the same thing at the same second, and neither of you will ever know, and that is precisely what makes it worth something.
